'''James Maxwell Bardeen''' (May 9, 1939 – June 20, 2022) was an American physicist. He worked on [[general relativity]], particularly in formulating the [[Black hole thermodynamics#The laws of black hole mechanics|laws of black hole mechanics]]. He also discovered the Bardeen vacuum, an [[Exact solutions in general relativity|exact solution]] of the [[Einstein field equation]].

==Early life and education==
Bardeen was born in [[Minneapolis]], [[Minnesota]], on May 9, 1939.<ref name="NYT obit">{{cite news|title=James Bardeen, an Expert on Unraveling Einstein's Equations, Dies at 83|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/07/03/science/space/james-bardeen-an-expert-on-unraveling-einsteins-equations-dies-at-83.html|first=Dennis|last=Overbye|date=July 3, 2022|access-date=July 3, 2022|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref>  His father, [[John Bardeen]], won the [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] twice for inventing the transistor and formulating the theory of superconductivity;<ref name="NYT obit"/><ref name=trueGenius>{{Cite book|title = True genius: the life and science of John Bardeen : the only winner of two Nobel Prizes in physics | first1=Lillian| last1=Hoddeson|first2=Vicki|last2=Daitch|publisher=Joseph Henry Press|year=2002 |isbn=978-0-309-08408-6 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZBQ7pmwfUyIC | page=93}}</ref> his mother, Jane Maxwell Bardeen, worked as a zoologist and a high school teacher.  During his childhood, Bardeen resided in [[Washington, D.C.]], [[Summit, New Jersey]], and [[Chicago]] as part of his father's employment.  He attended the [[University Laboratory High School (Urbana, Illinois)|University Laboratory High School]] in Urbana, Illinois.  He then studied physics at [[Harvard University]], even though his father wanted him to go into biology.<ref name="NYT obit"/>  After graduating in 1960, he undertook [[Postgraduate education|graduate studies]] at the [[California Institute of Technology]] under the direction of [[Richard Feynman]] and [[William Alfred Fowler]].<ref name="NYT obit"/><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://thesis.library.caltech.edu/view/author/Bardeen-J-M.html |title=Bardeen, James Maxwell – CaltechTHESIS |access-date=August 27, 2019 |archive-date=June 27, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210627005949/https://thesis.library.caltech.edu/view/author/Bardeen-J-M.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>  Bardeen was awarded a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] in 1965.<ref name="NYT obit"/>

==Career==
Bardeen first worked at Caltech and the [[University of California, Berkeley]], in postdoctoral positions.  He became a part of the astronomy department of the [[University of Washington]] in 1967.  He subsequently joined [[Yale University]] in 1972.  That same year, he co-authored the watershed paper "The Four Laws of Black Hole Mechanics" with [[Stephen Hawking]] and [[Brandon Carter]] during a meeting held at the [[École de physique des Houches]]. Later that year, Bardeen theorized the doughnut shape and size of a black hole’s shadow, which was later confirmed by the observations of [[Messier 87#Supermassive black hole M87*|M87*]] by the [[Event Horizon Telescope]].<ref name="NYT obit"/>

Bardeen returned to the University of Washington in 1976, remaining there until his retirement in 2006. Together with [[Michael S. Turner]] and [[Paul Steinhardt]], he published a paper in 1982 detailing the way submicroscopic fluctuations in the density of matter and energy in the [[Chronology of the universe#Early universe|early universe]] would bring about the arrangement of galaxies seen in the present day.<ref name="NYT obit"/>  Bardeen was also a distinguished visiting research fellow<ref>{{cite web|url=http://perimeterinstitute.ca/people/James-Bardeen|title=James Bardeen|website=Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics|access-date=January 12, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160421080141/http://perimeterinstitute.ca/people/James-Bardeen |archive-date=April 21, 2016}}</ref> at [[Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics]]. In 2012, he was elected to the U.S. [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11410007.html |title=James Maxwell Bardeen |work=Physics History Network |access-date=July 4, 2022}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Bardeen married Nancy Thomas in 1968.  They met the year before in [[Paris]] while he was attending a conference, and remained married until his death. Together, they had two children, William and David.<ref name="NYT obit" />

Bardeen's brother, [[William A. Bardeen]], was also a physicist.<ref name="NYT obit" />  His sister, Elizabeth, was married to [[Thomas Greytak]], a physicist at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]].  In a 2020 interview given to [[Federal University of Pará]] in Brazil, Bardeen recalls his journey as a physicist, his father's influences on him, his experiences as a doctoral student of Richard Feynman, and working with [[Stephen Hawking]].<ref>{{Cite AV media |title = Interview with Prof. James Bardeen – Part I|publisher=Federal University of Pará|year=2020 | url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=33gXiTui65Y |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211221/33gXiTui65Y |archive-date=December 21, 2021 |url-status=live}}{{cbignore}}</ref><ref>{{Cite AV media |title = Interview with Prof. James Bardeen – Part II|publisher=Federal University of Pará|year=2020 | url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BEcQdiuAMHk |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211221/BEcQdiuAMHk |archive-date=December 21, 2021 |url-status=live}}{{cbignore}}</ref><ref>{{Cite AV media |title = Interview with Prof. James Bardeen – Part III|publisher=Federal University of Pará|year=2020 | url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DdTJSzux0cU |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211221/DdTJSzux0cU |archive-date=December 21, 2021 |url-status=live}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

Bardeen died on June 20, 2022, at a retirement home in [[Seattle]].  He was 83, and suffered from cancer prior to his death.<ref name="NYT obit"/>
